Hook: A bed net treated with insecticide costs a few dollars, and a child who sleeps under one is far less likely to catch malaria. For years donors argued over how to hand them out. One side said: sell them, cheaply. People who pay for a net are people who value it, and they will hang it up and use it; a free net may end up as a fishing net. The other side said: give them away. More people will be covered, and a net protects the neighbours too, because it kills the mosquitoes. In Kenya, Jessica Cohen and Pascaline Dupas settled it with an experiment. At 20 prenatal clinics, they drew the price at random, from free up to 40 shillings, about sixty cents. At sixty cents, demand fell by about 60 percent. And the women who paid were no more likely to use their nets than the women who got one free.

The Island runs the same experiment at its own clinic. In gold, the share of mothers who take a net at each price. Free, nearly all of them. At sixty cents, 36 percent: a fall of 62 percent, as in Kenya. In green, the share who take a net and sleep under it. Of those who take one, 65 percent use it, whatever they paid. So charging does not pick out the users; it just leaves fewer people protected. If paying had screened for use, the share using their nets would rise with the price, from 71 to 88 percent. That is the question the experiment answered, and the answer is in the data, not in the argument.

This part asks why the poor stay poor, and what actually helps. Who is poor, and how would we count them across a world of different prices? Is poverty a trap, from which people cannot climb out on their own, or only a slow start? Which markets fail the poor, and why: credit, insurance, land and labour? And what do cash, schools, medicine and loans actually do, and how could anyone know?

Here is the plan. How the world counts its poor, an aid budget for you to spend, and whether poverty is a trap. The farm and the town; what credit and cash do, and a programme built for the very poorest. Schools, health, risk, fertilizer and mobile money, and history that is still visible in today's incomes. The debate over what experiments can teach, with real data from four of them. Three dials, the people who use these ideas, and the frontier.
Counting: How do you count the world's poor? The World Bank's recipe has five steps. Start from the poverty lines that the poorest countries set for themselves, each in its own currency. Convert them at purchasing-power parity: not the market exchange rate, but the rate at which a dollar buys the same basket of goods in each country, from the price surveys of Part three. That gives one line for the whole world, in 1990 about a dollar a day. Then take household surveys, which record what each household consumes. And count the people below the line. Every step needs prices, and the prices are the hard part.

The line has been re-set five times since 1990, each time new prices arrived from the International Comparison Program. A dollar a day at 1985 prices; one dollar 8 at 1993 prices; one dollar 25 at 2005 prices; one dollar 90 at 2011 prices; two dollars 15 at 2017 prices; and, since June 2025, three dollars at 2021 prices. Each re-set can move the count. In 2008 Shaohua Chen and Martin Ravallion reported that 1.4 billion people had been poor in 2005, about 400 million more than the old prices had said. Nobody had become poorer; the prices were new. The 2025 update raised the count again, and the World Bank was careful to say the same thing: a higher line, not a poorer world.

Here is the count at the new line, from the World Bank's own data. In 1981, 47 percent of the world's people lived on less than three dollars a day at today's prices. By 2024, 10 percent. Most of the fall happened in East Asia, from 77 percent to 2. Then South Asia, from 56 percent to 2.6. Sub-Saharan Africa started at 62 percent in 1990, and is at 45 percent. With its population growing fast, the number of poor people there has risen, and most of the world's poor now live there.

Two countries carry most of the story. In China, 97 percent of people were below the line in 1981; by 2018, under one percent. India: 51 percent in 1983, and 2.6 percent in the latest survey. The dots are the survey years. India's surveys are years apart, and its survey's design changed for 2022 and 2023, so the last steps are less certain than the line suggests. No randomized experiment produced either fall. They came with decades of growth, in farms, factories and cities. Keep that in mind when this part turns to experiments: they answer smaller questions very well.

In his 2010 presidential address to the American Economic Association, Angus Deaton listed what can go wrong. Whose basket? The price comparisons weigh goods by what everyone in a country buys, not what the poor buy. Which year? Each new round of prices redraws the map, as the 2008 round did. Which survey? Some countries measure consumption, others income, and the two are not the same. His conclusion was not that the count is worthless. The fall in poverty since 1980 survives every choice; the exact level, and the ranking of regions, are softer than the decimal points suggest.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: spend the aid budget.

Your turn. You run the Island's aid agency, with ten million dollars to spend this year, and six programmes to spend it on. Each curve shows what a programme achieves as you spend more on it, measured in one common unit, thousands of years of healthy life. Deworming, cash transfers, bed nets, remedial tutoring, microcredit, and a graduation programme for the poorest. The steepness at the start is what the first million buys. Bed nets are the steepest. But every curve flattens. The first nets go to the villages with the most malaria; the next million reaches places where it does less good.

Three plans. Plan A: put all ten million into the best programme, bed nets. Plan B: spread it evenly, one and two-thirds million to each. Plan C: your own split. Pause, and decide where your money goes.

Here is what each plan buys. Plan A, everything on nets: 5.0 thousand healthy years. The nets run out of good places to go long before the money runs out. Plan B, equal shares: 18.6. Spreading the money does far better. The best split buys 19.8. It funds five programmes, in different amounts, and gives nothing to microcredit, whose first million buys less than the last million spent anywhere else. How close did your own split come?

The rule behind the best split is Part five's, applied to a budget. Keep moving money to whichever programme buys the most with its next dollar, until the next dollar buys the same everywhere it is spent. At the best split, the last million spent on each funded programme buys about 1.23 thousand years. Microcredit's very first million buys only 0.80, so it gets nothing. The lesson is that cost-effectiveness is a number at the margin, not an average. The charity evaluator GiveWell asks not only how much good a charity does per dollar, but how much more money it could use as well: its room for more funding. The rest of this part is about what goes into curves like these, and how anyone could measure them.
Traps: A trap needs a reason why a little more capital does little, but a lot more does a lot. On the Island the reason is a choice of technology. A household with little can farm a plot with a hoe: output is the square root of its capital. Or it can buy into something better, a cow, a cart, a small shop, which produces four times the square root, less a fixed cost of eleven: the cow must be bought whole. The better technology pays only above a capital of 13.4. Below that, the household is better off with the hoe.

Now let households save. Each year a household saves 30 percent of its output, and loses 10 percent of its capital to wear and death. Here is how much its capital changes over a year, at each level of capital. Above the dashed line capital grows; below it, capital shrinks. The curve crosses the line three times. At 9, a low steady state: the hoe, forever. At 60, a high one. And between them, at 18.2, a threshold. Start below it and capital drifts down to the low state; start above it and it climbs to the high one. Two households with the same skills and the same patience end up in different worlds, because of where they started. That is a poverty trap.

Here are the Island's households, three thousand of them, with capital around ten and good and bad years along the way. Forty of each are drawn. With no help, 9 percent start above the threshold, and after 12 years 9 percent are above it. The rest stay where they began. Now give each household a one-off transfer of ten, about what it already owns. 67 percent are pushed across the threshold, and after 12 years 58 percent are above it, climbing. Those it did not push across slide back, as if it had never happened. A transfer of twenty pushes everyone across, and 97 percent are above it twelve years later. In a trap, the size of a transfer matters in a way it does not in Part twenty's Solow model: a small one is spent, a large one changes a life.

Do real households face traps like this? For years the answer was: rarely. In 2014 Aart Kraay and David McKenzie reviewed the evidence for each kind of trap in the models, and found little for most of them; the strongest case was for places, remote or unhealthy regions, more than for households. The test is the one the Island just ran: give households a large asset at random, and see who keeps climbing. Clare Balboni, Oriana Bandiera, Robin Burgess, Maitreesh Ghatak and Anton Heil followed six thousand households in rural Bangladesh for eleven years, half of them given cows by the charity BRAC at random. They found a threshold. Households that ended up above a certain level of assets kept accumulating and moved into better work; those below slid back. And they estimate that the trap wastes 15 times what it would cost, once, to push households across it.
Dual: In 1954 W. Arthur Lewis, who would share a Nobel prize for it, described how a poor economy grows. Most people work on family farms, where there is more labour than land: take one worker away and the harvest barely changes. A modern sector, factories and mines and trade, can hire from the farms at a wage just above subsistence, and workers come without a raise. Its owners reinvest their profits, which creates more jobs at the same wage, year after year, as long as the surplus on the farms lasts. When it runs out, the modern sector must bid workers away from farms that now miss them, and wages begin to rise. That moment is called the Lewis turning point.

Here is Lewis's economy on the Island: a hundred workers, sixty of them surplus on the farms. Modern employment grows slowly, then fast, as reinvested profits compound. Through all of it, the wage stays at subsistence. Growth goes to profits, and to more jobs, not to higher pay. In year 28 the surplus is used up. From then on each worker the factories hire is missed on the farm, the wage rises, and the gains of growth begin to reach workers. Many economists have asked whether China passed its own turning point in the 2000s, when factory wages there began to climb fast.

Lewis's dual economy leaves a trace in national accounts. If farms hold more workers than they need, output per worker on farms is low compared with output per worker elsewhere. The ratio is easy to compute: the share of value added outside farms over the share of workers outside farms, divided by the same ratio on farms. Here it is for 172 countries, from the World Bank's latest data. In the poorest quarter of countries the median worker outside agriculture produces 2.8 times as much as one on a farm. In the richest quarter, 1.7 times. If labour moved freely to where it produces most, the ratio would be about one. In poor countries it is far from one.

Douglas Gollin, David Lagakos and Michael Waugh asked how much of this gap is real. In national accounts it is about three, and larger in developing countries. Part of it is measurement: farmers work fewer hours, have less schooling, live where things cost less, and grow food that surveys miss. Correct for all of it, and a gap of about two remains. Why would workers leave that much on the table? Either the people who move are different from those who stay, so the gap is about people rather than places; or something stops them moving, the cost of a city, the loss of village insurance, rights to land that lapse when you leave. Which one it is decides whether helping people move to towns would raise their incomes, and Part thirty-seven's cities are part of the answer.
Credit: In villages, moneylenders often charge rates that look like exploitation. In 1990 Irfan Aleem studied 14 of them around the market town of Chambar in Pakistan. They charged about 78 percent a year on average. Where does a rate like that come from? A lender who breaks even must get back, from the borrowers who repay, the cost of its own money plus the cost of finding good borrowers and chasing the rest. On the Island the lender's own money costs 10 percent. 15 percent of loans are never repaid, which adds 19 points. And screening and collection, the lender's time and travel, add 24 more: 53 percent in all. Aleem found his lenders' rates were close to what their lending cost them. The high price of credit is mostly the high cost of information, not monopoly profit.

If information is the problem, who has it? The neighbours. In 1976 Muhammad Yunus began lending to poor villagers in Bangladesh, and the Grameen Bank he founded lent to small groups, mostly of women, meeting every week. In the classic design each member is liable for the others' loans. So the group chooses its members, and watches them, using what neighbours know and a bank does not. Repayment was high without any collateral, and the rates, though high by a bank's standards, were below the moneylender's. Microcredit spread across the world, with the promise that it would lift its borrowers out of poverty. That is a claim an experiment can test.

Here is the test, run on the Island. A microlender opens in villages drawn at random, charging 25 percent a year. In the planted truth, 15 percent of the villagers' businesses would earn 60 percent a year on more capital, and the rest only 5, less than the loan costs. 32 percent of the people offered a loan take one: the high-return businesses, and some others who borrow to buy a roof or get through a bad month. The average effect on profits is 4.0 on a mean of 218, about 2 percent. Per borrower, 12.4. Modest. And yet a few businesses are doing very well.

An average hides where the effect is. Compare the whole distribution of profits in villages with the lender against villages without it, percentile by percentile: the median against the median, the ninetieth percentile against the ninetieth. The shading is a ninety-five percent band from resampling households. Over most of the distribution, nothing changes: the band includes zero. At the top, large gains. Microcredit is not useless and not transformative; it works for the few businesses with somewhere productive to put the money. The real studies found exactly this shape.

In 2015 the American Economic Journal published six randomized evaluations of microcredit together, from Bosnia, Ethiopia, India, Mexico, Mongolia and Morocco. Abhijit Banerjee, Dean Karlan and Jonathan Zinman summed them up: effects modestly positive, but not transformative. Rachael Meager pooled seven trials with a hierarchical model and reached the same conclusion, adding that about 60 percent of the differences between sites was just noise, which means the trials agree more than they seem to. The gains were concentrated among people who already ran businesses. Which leaves a puzzle. When researchers simply gave cash grants to small firms in Sri Lanka, at random, the firms earned 4.6 to 5.3 percent a month on it. If capital is that productive, why does credit do so little? The answer, for the most part, is that the average borrower is not the average grant recipient, and that returns vary enormously between firms. Chapter fourteen's first dial collects them.
Cash: In 1997 Mexico's government launched PROGRESA. Poor mothers were paid every two months, on condition that their children went to school, with larger grants for older children, who were the ones most likely to leave, and that the family visited the health clinic. The money could not reach every village at once, and the designers, led by the economist Santiago Levy, turned that into an experiment: 320 of 506 localities, drawn at random, started in 1998, and the rest later. Paul Schultz used the comparison to measure the effect on schooling. Primary enrolment was already high and barely moved. The gains came after primary school, exactly where children had been dropping out, and he put the return on the grants, counted as extra schooling, at about eight percent a year. The design, conditional cash transfers with an evaluation built in, was copied across Latin America and beyond.

Then came a simpler question: what if there are no conditions at all? The charity GiveDirectly sends money to poor households in rural Kenya by mobile phone. Johannes Haushofer and Jeremy Shapiro evaluated it with a randomized trial. Households received 404 or 1,525 dollars at purchasing-power parity. About nine months on, monthly consumption was 193 dollars, against 158 in the control group, and households owned more and reported less stress. They did not spend it on alcohol or tobacco, a common fear about handing out cash. But in a follow-up three years later, the gains in consumption were no longer evident. Cash helps; whether it lasts is a different question.

A transfer does not stop at the household that receives it. On the Island, a household spends it, and 75 percent of what it spends goes to sellers in the same village, who spend 80 percent of what they earn: 0.60 of every dollar comes back as someone else's income. And again, 0.36, and so on. This is Part twenty-seven's multiplier, at the scale of a village: one over one minus 0.60, or 2.5. If local sellers could not produce more, the extra demand would raise prices instead; here a little of it does, and the real multiplier is 2.47. Dennis Egger, Johannes Haushofer, Edward Miguel, Paul Niehaus and Michael Walker measured it, by randomizing how many households in each area received GiveDirectly's transfers: over 10,500 households in 653 villages, more than fifteen percent of local GDP. The multiplier was about 2.5, prices rose by about a tenth of a percent, and neighbours who received nothing gained too.

Cash also changes politics. Between 2005 and 2007 Uruguay paid a monthly transfer to households below a cutoff in a poverty score computed from a survey. Households just below and just above the cutoff are alike in every way except eligibility, which makes Part four's regression discontinuity possible. Here are 1,948 of them, from data Marco Manacorda, Edward Miguel and Andrea Vigorito collected, grouped by score. On the left, the eligible, all of whom took part. On the right, those just too well off. At the cutoff, support for the government jumps by 10 points, with a standard error of 3, computed here by local linear regression on each side. The authors' own estimates were 11 to 14 points. People notice who helps them, which is one reason governments like cash transfers, and one reason to design them by rule.
Graduation: Microcredit did little for the poorest, who had no business to lend to. In Bangladesh the charity BRAC designed something else for them. A productive asset, goats or a cow or the stock for a small shop. Training in how to keep it alive and earning. Cash or food for the first months, so the asset is not sold or eaten. A savings account. And a coach who visits every week, for a year or two. It is expensive, and it is meant to happen once: a big push, aimed at exactly the threshold of chapter three. The name is graduation: from aid, into a livelihood.

Would it work outside Bangladesh? Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, Dean Karlan, Christopher Udry and their coauthors ran the same programme as six randomized trials, in Ethiopia, Ghana, Honduras, India, Pakistan and Peru, with about 21,000 people. A year after the programme ended, consumption was higher in 5 of the six sites. Honduras was the exception. And in 5 of the six, the benefits were larger than the costs. A programme designed in one country, run by different organizations on three continents, mostly worked. That is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence that, for the very poorest, a large push can do what small help cannot.

This is how Balboni and her coauthors found their threshold, and it can be done on the Island. Give every household a transfer of ten. Across, each household's capital just after the transfer; up the side, how much it changed over the next twelve years. Households that end up below the threshold lose ground: the transfer is slowly eaten. Those above it climb, slowly at first, toward the high steady state. The median change, in gold, crosses zero near the threshold. In Bangladesh, with real households and real cows, the curve had the same shape. Here, 66 percent were pushed across. A larger transfer would push more, which is why the size of the push, not only whether there is one, is the policy question.
Schools: Between 1973 and 1979, with money from the oil boom, Indonesia's government built more than 61,000 primary schools. Esther Duflo found an experiment in the way they were placed. More schools went to regions where fewer children had been enrolled, so some regions got many and others few. And only children young enough to attend could benefit; those already past primary school age could not. So compare young and old where many schools were built, and young and old where few were: a difference in differences, as in Part four. Each new school per thousand children raised schooling by 0.12 to 0.19 years, and later wages by 1.5 to 2.7 percent. Divide one by the other and you have the return to a year of school.

The Island builds schools the same way, in 280 regions. Each dot is a region: across, how many schools it got; up the side, how much more schooling its young cohort has than its old one. The more schools, the bigger the gap, by 0.155 years per school. The same for wages, measured years later: 0.0148 in log wages per school. The ratio is the return to a year of school, an instrumental-variables estimate of the kind in Part four, with the schools as the instrument: 0.095, against a planted 0.08. Duflo's own estimates ran from about seven to eleven percent, and a recent reanalysis by David Roodman argues their uncertainty was understated. Chapter fourteen adds both to the dial.

Building schools raised enrolment across the poor world. Learning is another matter. The World Bank counts a child in learning poverty if, at ten, they cannot read and understand a simple text. In 2022 it estimated that 70 percent of ten-year-olds in low- and middle-income countries were in learning poverty, up from 57 percent before the pandemic closed schools. Many of these children are in school. The curriculum moves on whether or not they keep up, and the teacher teaches to the top of the class. Children who fell behind in the second year can sit through the fifth understanding little.

The Indian organization Pratham built a response, called Teaching at the Right Level. Test every child quickly: can they read a letter, a word, a short story? For an hour or two a day, group children by what they can do, not by their grade. Teach what each group is ready to learn. Test again and regroup every few weeks. Randomized evaluations with Banerjee and Duflo found language gains of 0.15 standard deviations where government teachers ran it for an hour a day in Haryana, and 0.7 where volunteers ran short intensive camps in Uttar Pradesh. In two other states, where teachers did not adopt the method, it achieved little: the idea works only if someone actually changes how the class is taught.
Health: Intestinal worms infect hundreds of millions of children, leaving them tired and anaemic. A pill twice a year, given at school, costs a few cents a dose. The worms spread through soil contaminated by infected children, so treating one child means fewer eggs around the school, and that protects classmates who took no pill. That spillover makes a careful design essential. Edward Miguel and Michael Kremer randomized whole schools, 75 of them in Busia in western Kenya, phased in over several years. Deworming cut absence from school by a quarter, and pupils who were not treated, in treated schools and nearby ones, gained as well. Test scores did not measurably change.

The Island's schools show why. In control schools, children miss 27 percent of days. Compare, within treated schools, the pupils who took the pill with those who did not: absence is 6.7 points lower. But the untreated pupils in treated schools are themselves 4.3 points better off than pupils in control schools, because there are fewer worms around them. So the comparison within a school understates what the pill does to each treated child, and misses entirely what it does for the others. Compare whole schools, and the programme cuts absence by 9.3 points for every pupil enrolled. Where there is no spillover, the within-school comparison would have been the right one. A design must match how the treatment spreads.

The result made deworming one of the most recommended charities in the world, and then it was attacked. In 2004, absence down by a quarter, with spillovers. In 2015 two teams of epidemiologists re-analysed the data, which the authors had shared, and published in the International Journal of Epidemiology. They found coding errors, and argued that with other reasonable choices the attendance effects were much weaker. The press called it the worm wars. The authors replied that after the corrections the main results, including the spillovers, still held, and that the disagreement was mostly about methods. Economists and epidemiologists still disagree about parts of it. But the episode is a model of how evidence should work: data shared, analyses repeated, and the argument conducted in the open.

Prices matter in the other direction too. In rural Malawi in 2004, Rebecca Thornton's team offered free HIV tests at people's homes; to learn the result, people had to walk to a clinic later. Each person drew a voucher worth between nothing and about three dollars, to be paid on collecting the result. Here are her data, 2,834 people. With no incentive, 34 percent went. With any incentive, 79 percent. And the first few cents did most of the work: a voucher worth under a quarter of a dollar raised the share to 64 percent. The nets in the hook were the same lesson in reverse. For goods that protect health, the step between free and almost free matters more than any later step.

Distance acts like a price. Thornton's team also placed the clinics at random, so the distance people had to walk was as good as drawn by lottery. Of those within a kilometre, 74 percent collected their result; of those three to five kilometres away, 65. A walk costs hours, and for people who earn by the day, hours are money. Many of the cheapest ways to help are ways of making the right choice a little easier, a little closer, or a little cheaper.
Risk: Poor households face huge risks, a failed harvest, a sick cow, an illness, and almost none of them have insurance policies. Yet they are not helpless. When one household is hit, neighbours and relatives send gifts and lend money, repaid when times are good. If this works, a household's consumption should follow the fortunes of the village, which nobody can insure against locally, and not its own luck. The village insures its members, without a single contract. In 1994 Robert Townsend turned this into a test. Regress the change in a household's consumption on the change in its own income, holding the village's fortunes fixed with a separate effect for each village and year. With full insurance the slope is zero; with none, it is one.

On the Island, the share of a household's own shocks that its village absorbs is planted, so the test can be checked. In gold, Townsend's slope, across villages that pool none, a quarter, a half, eighty-five percent or all of their members' shocks. It recovers one minus the pooled share exactly. In red, the same regression without the village-year effects. Now the shocks that hit the whole village, which no neighbour can insure, show up as a lack of insurance. With eighty-five percent pooling, the right slope is 0.15, the wrong one 0.25. In three villages in semi-arid India, Townsend rejected full insurance, but found consumption much closer to it than to none: a good benchmark, with holes, for the poorest and for the largest shocks.

What the village cannot insure is the shock that hits everyone at once, like a drought. That is what rainfall insurance is for: it pays when a rain gauge records a drought, so no claims adjuster has to visit, and nobody can cheat. Development economists were enthusiastic. Farmers were not. On the Island, a drought comes one year in 5 and takes half the harvest. Priced fairly and trusted, a risk-averse farmer buys full cover when the gauge is perfect, and less as basis risk grows: the chance that the farm suffers a drought the gauge does not record, or the gauge pays when the farm is fine. Add a premium 30 percent above the expected payout, and demand falls. And if farmers believe the insurer will pay only 80 percent of the time, the cover they want falls to nothing at high basis risk. In India, Shawn Cole and his coauthors found take-up of 5 to 10 percent at market prices, sensitive to the price and to whether farmers trusted the seller. Insurance is a promise, and promises from strangers are worth less.

Jing Cai, Alain de Janvry and Elisabeth Sadoulet studied a new weather insurance for rice farmers in rural China. Here are 1,410 of their households, from 166 villages. At the end of each information session, farmers were given a default at random: either they would be signed up unless they said no, or not signed up unless they said yes. Where the default was to buy, 52 percent bought; where it was not, 41: a difference of 11 points, with a standard error of 3, computed here. Part forty-five's defaults, in a Chinese village. Their main finding was about networks: for a farmer not trained directly, one more friend who had been through the intensive session raised take-up as much as a 15 percent cut in the premium. People learn what insurance is from people they trust.
Farms: Chapter eleven. Farms, phones and firms.

In western Kenya, fertilizer used in modest amounts pays well, yet most farmers do not use it. Esther Duflo, Michael Kremer and Jonathan Robinson asked why. At harvest a farmer has cash, and means to buy fertilizer, but the trip to town can wait. By planting time the cash has gone, on school fees, food, or a funeral. And another season passes without it. That is Part forty-five's present bias, in a field. So they offered farmers, right after harvest, a voucher for fertilizer at the regular price, with free delivery later. No discount: just the chance to commit while the money was there. Among 1,230 farmers, use rose by 14 points, from 24 percent. The same offer made later in the season had no significant effect, and the harvest-time offer did about as much as a fifty percent subsidy offered later.

The Island's farmers have the same problem, with a planted present bias. With no offer, 24 percent use fertilizer. Offer free delivery right after harvest, at the regular price, and 35 percent do. The offer removes the trip at the one moment the cash is there. Offer the same thing at planting, and nothing changes: 24 percent. The cash is already gone. Cutting the price in half at planting does about as much as the free harvest offer, 37 percent, at far greater cost. And if every farmer were patient, 39 percent would use fertilizer with no offer at all. The gap is procrastination, and timing closes much of it for almost nothing.

Some technologies spread without any help. In 2007 Kenya's largest phone company launched M-PESA, which lets anyone with a basic phone store and send money by text, through agents in shops in almost every village. William Jack and Tavneet Suri found that households using it kept their consumption up after a bad shock, because relatives far away could send money the same day. Chapter ten's village insurance, stretched across a country. Later, using how far each household lived from the nearest agent, Suri and Jack estimated that mobile money had lifted about 194,000 households, two percent of Kenya's, out of extreme poverty, and helped about 185,000 women move from farming into business or retail.

Firms leave money on the table too. Nicholas Bloom, David McKenzie and their coauthors chose Indian textile plants at random and gave them free consulting on basic practices: recording defects, organizing inventory, maintaining machines. Productivity rose 17 percent in the first year, and within three years the treated firms were opening more plants. Why had the owners not done it already? Mostly, they did not know what they were missing. Part sixty-two returns to management as a technology.
History: In 1573 the Spanish rulers of Peru imposed the mita. Villages had to send one in seven of their adult men to work in the silver mines of Potosí and the mercury mines of Huancavelica, under brutal conditions. The obligation applied only to villages inside a boundary drawn by colonial administrators; villages just outside were exempt. The mita was abolished in 1812, more than two centuries ago. Melissa Dell compared districts just inside the old boundary with districts just outside it, with the same altitude, soils and ethnic make-up. Inside, household consumption today is about 25 percent lower, and children are about 6 points more likely to be stunted.

The Island has an old boundary too, with a planted effect. Each dot is the average log consumption of districts in a ten-kilometre band, inside the old boundary on the left. Consumption rises gently from left to right everywhere, as land gets lower and closer to the coast. Fit a line on each side, using only districts within 50 kilometres of the boundary. The gap between the lines at the boundary is minus 0.277 in logs, close to the planted minus 0.25. A regression discontinuity across a line on a map works like the one across a cutoff in a score: neighbours on either side are compared, and whatever changes smoothly with distance cancels out.

How does a labour rule abolished in 1812 lower incomes today? Dell's answer is land. Large estates, haciendas, formed mostly outside the boundary, where they did not have to compete with the mita for workers. Their owners had the political connections to get roads built, and those roads still carry farmers' produce to market. Inside the boundary, there are fewer roads, and more families farm only to feed themselves. A caution from Part nineteen: studies that regress one map on another can find persistence in what is really spatial noise. A discontinuity at a boundary, comparing near neighbours, is much less exposed to that problem, which is why Dell's design is so admired.

The largest example is Africa's slave trades. Nathan Nunn assembled shipping and census records to estimate how many people were taken from each part of Africa over five centuries. The countries from which the most slaves were taken are the poorest today. That could be because poorer places were raided more, so he used the sailing distance from each country to the slave markets of the Americas and the Indian Ocean as an instrument, and the relationship survived. With Leonard Wantchekon he found one channel: people from the ethnic groups raided most heavily trust others less today, a belief passed down from a time when neighbours and even relatives might sell you.
Debate: Chapter thirteen. The debate over experiments.

Most of this part has rested on randomized experiments, and that is new. For decades development economics asked big questions, like why some countries are poor, that no experiment can answer. From the 1990s, starting with Michael Kremer's school trials in Kenya, a new generation broke them into small ones: does this pill, this price, this kind of teaching, work? Randomize, and measure. Thousands of trials have followed. Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo's book Poor Economics argued that answers built up this way, one question at a time, change policy more than grand theories. In 2019 the three of them shared the Nobel prize, for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty.

The approach has serious critics, and the most eloquent is Angus Deaton, himself a Nobel laureate. A randomized trial measures an average effect, in one place, at one time, with one organization running the programme. Whether it holds anywhere else is a separate question, which randomization does nothing to answer. A programme scaled up to a whole country changes prices and wages, as chapter six's multiplier did, and is run by a government rather than a motivated charity. And a result without a model of why it worked cannot tell you what will happen when anything changes. None of this says experiments are useless. It says they are a beginning, not an end.

Here is the problem in numbers. The Island runs the same programme in 12 places, and evaluates each with a good trial, a standard error of 0.05. The estimates, with their intervals, spread far more widely than their errors allow. The average is 0.18, but the true effects themselves differ from place to place, with a spread estimated at 0.12, larger than any trial's error. Statistics, Built's shrinkage pulls each estimate toward the average, by more where the trial is noisy relative to that spread. And for the next place, where no trial has been run, the honest forecast runs from minus 0.06 to 0.42: it could be harmful, or twice the average. The precision of each trial does not carry over. Eva Vivalt, collecting hundreds of impact evaluations, found exactly this: large differences between studies of the same kind of programme, with smaller effects when governments, rather than researchers or charities, ran them.

And there is the elephant in the room. In four decades China lifted close to 800 million people out of extreme poverty, about 75 percent of the fall in the whole world, by the World Bank's count. No randomized trial produced it. It came with the reform of farms, factories built for export, and hundreds of millions of people moving to cities, the subjects of Parts twenty, twenty-one, thirty-five and thirty-seven. The two traditions answer different questions. Experiments say what works in a village, and how much; growth decides how many villages are poor in the first place. A serious development economist needs both.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: evaluators, development banks, and cost-effectiveness.

Who uses development economics? Evaluators: the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, founded at MIT in 2003, Innovations for Poverty Action, and the World Bank's own impact evaluation teams, who design and run trials with governments and charities. The development banks, which lend to governments for roads, schools and transfer programmes, and must decide what to fund. Governments, whose ministries run the programmes at a scale no charity can. Charities and the foundations that fund them. And economists in every one of these places, designing the trials, reading the evidence, and turning it into budgets.

Here is cost-effectiveness done in public. The charity evaluator GiveWell publishes its arithmetic. A bed net costs about 6 dollars, bought and delivered. It estimates how many children each net protects, allowing for how many are used and for how long. And how many deaths that averts, from malaria's toll where the nets go. For the Against Malaria Foundation it arrives at about 5,500 dollars per life saved, for its grants from 2022 to 2024, and calls the number a rough estimate. The same arithmetic is done for deworming, cash and other programmes, on one scale, and then, as in chapter two, GiveWell asks how much more money each could use as well. The numbers are uncertain. Writing them down is what makes them arguable, and so improvable.

Called it? In 2005 Jeffrey Sachs published The End of Poverty. He argued that extreme poverty could be ended by 2025, if rich countries raised their aid to between 135 and 195 billion dollars a year and spent it on health, schools, farms and roads. His Millennium Villages project was meant to show how. Here is the share of the world below the line of three dollars a day, from 2005, when it was 28 percent. Aid rose, but never to the share of rich countries' incomes his plan required. Poverty fell fast, mostly in Asia and mostly with growth, but in 2025 about 808 million people still lived below the line, one in ten. The Millennium Villages' final evaluation found gains on thirty of forty outcomes, with poverty itself less conclusive. The verdict: wrong. The goal was a good one, and the forecast underrated how hard it is to buy development from outside.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: scaling, satellites and phones.

The first frontier is a reply to Deaton. Karthik Muralidharan and Paul Niehaus argued for running experiments at the scale at which policy is made. Randomize the unit a government actually decides about, whole districts or states, not a handful of villages. Measure what happens to markets, prices and wages, not only to the people treated, as the Kenyan cash study did. Let the government's own staff run the programme, since they will run it afterwards. And study the politics of what survives. A trial built this way answers much of the critique, at the cost of being much harder to run.

The second frontier is measurement. Household surveys are slow and expensive, and many poor countries go years without one. Start instead from a few thousand surveyed households, and train a model to recognise wealth in other data: satellite images of night lights, roofs and roads, or the records of mobile phones, who calls whom and how much credit they buy. Then predict wealth everywhere else, and draw a map of poverty in weeks. Neal Jean and his coauthors explained up to 75 percent of the variation in local wealth across five African countries from satellite images. Joshua Blumenstock and his coauthors mapped wealth across Rwanda from the phone records of 1.5 million subscribers, trained on just 856 surveyed people.

In April 2020, as the pandemic closed markets, Togo's government wanted to send emergency cash to its poorest people, and had no register of who they were. Emily Aiken, Suzanne Bellue, Dean Karlan, Chris Udry and Joshua Blumenstock helped target it from phone records. The Island can show the trade-off. A transfer meant for the poorest 30 percent, given at random, misses 70 percent of them. Given to the poorest villages, it misses 52 percent, because many poor people live in villages that are not poor on average. Ranked by a prediction from phone records, 48 percent. A full survey of every household would miss 33 percent, but would take years. In Togo, the phone method cut exclusion errors by 4 to 21 percent against the geographic options the government considered, and did worse than a full registry would have. The frontier is to make such tools accurate, fair, and accountable to the people they sort.
